vectors.name: osd-grammar/strings/label-unescaping-has-no-named-escape-table
vectors.comment: OSD string unescaping replaces every backslash pair \X with the literal character X; there is no named-escape table, so \n becomes the letter n, not a newline. The label is the three-character string "anb".

vectors.name: osd-grammar/cardinality/at-least-m-unbounded
vectors.comment: The comma-first-with-trailing-bound form: at least 5, unbounded above.

vectors.name: osd-grammar/cardinality/comma-first-at-most-n
vectors.comment: The comma-first form: no minimum bound is required before the comma. min=0, max=5.

vectors.name: osd-grammar/cardinality/comma-only-any-count
vectors.comment: Any count, including zero -- min=0, max=unbounded.

vectors.name: osd-grammar/cardinality/negative-minimum-is-invalid-not-a-syntax-error
vectors.comment: [-1] MUST surface as the invalid-cardinality error, never a bare syntax/parse error -- whether the tokenizer rejects the '-' at the token boundary or accepts it and field construction rejects it one step later is an implementation choice, not an observable difference.

vectors.name: osd-grammar/cardinality/inverted-range-is-invalid
vectors.comment: [1,0] tokenizes fine (both are plain unsigned ints) and is rejected only at field construction, once max < min is checked.

vectors.name: osd-grammar/cardinality/zero-max-is-invalid-redundant-with-absence
vectors.comment: [0,0] tokenizes fine and passes the negative/inverted-range checks (0 is non-negative, max == min is not inverted), but is rejected anyway: a field that must occur exactly zero times is indistinguishable, in every observable respect, from a field that was never declared -- an undeclared label present in a document is already validate.unexpected-field. [0,0] would be a second spelling for that same thing, which this spec does not permit anywhere else (Sec4.3.1's empty-array-vs-absent-label rule is the same principle).

vectors.name: osd-grammar/labels/empty-label-is-rejected
vectors.comment: "" is a legal *value* for an OML/OSD string generally, but a label is an identifier, not a value -- an empty label names nothing a caller could ever reference. Path is R (the label-itself-is-the-problem case), the same convention osd-grammar/labels/unquoted-field-name-is-rejected already uses, since there's no usable label to append as R.<label>.

vectors.name: osd-grammar/nullable/question-mark-on-a-reference-is-rejected
vectors.comment: ? MUST NOT follow a reference; the error MUST point the author at cardinality [0,1] instead -- 'this subtree may be absent' is a cardinality question, not a nullability question.

vectors.name: osd-grammar/any/any-with-question-mark-is-rejected
vectors.comment: any already includes null, so a nullable-any suffix is redundant rather than meaningful and is rejected outright.

vectors.name: osd-grammar/any/capitalized-any-is-an-ordinary-reference
vectors.comment: Only the exact lowercase spelling `any` is reserved. Capitalized `Any` is an ordinary name and therefore a reference -- it fails here only because no record named Any is defined, not because of any reservation.

vectors.name: osd-grammar/reserved-names/record-named-after-a-scalar-keyword-is-rejected
vectors.comment: A bare name in type position resolves to the builtin scalar keyword first, so a record named `string` could never be referenced.

vectors.name: osd-grammar/root/missing-root-is-an-error
vectors.comment: Sec8.4 defines Schema paths as RecordName/RecordName.label, with no whole-schema form -- there is no specific record to name when the schema has no root at all, so $ is used here as a defensible fallback pending the spec's own clarification of this case.

vectors.name: osd-grammar/root/duplicate-root-is-an-error
vectors.comment: Ledger entry DIV-2 (closed; divergence-ledger numbering, not chapter 2's D-N rules): a second root declaration used to be permitted to silently win over the first in at least one implementation. Sec5.8 now MUSTs a schema have exactly one root declaration; a second is an error, not an override. Path is $ for the same reason as osd-grammar/root/missing-root-is-an-error -- there is no specific record to blame, the schema itself is malformed.

vectors.name: osd-grammar/labels/unquoted-field-name-is-rejected
vectors.comment: The quoting rule has no exceptions: a bare name in label position is always an error, since a bare name is reserved for schema-name position (scalar keyword, any, or a reference).

vectors.name: osd-grammar/labels/quoted-string-in-type-position-is-rejected
vectors.comment: The other direction of the same quoting rule (omnist-spec#35): a quoted string is a data string, reserved for label position -- it can never appear in type position, where only a bare schema name (scalar keyword, any, or a reference) is legal. Confirmed live that the reference implementation already rejects this; schema.quoted-type is the code this vector pins as the target, symmetric with schema.unquoted-label above.

vectors.name: osd-grammar/any/cardinality-is-orthogonal-to-any
vectors.comment: any and cardinality are independent axes; opening a field to any does not restrict what cardinality it may carry.

vectors.name: osd-grammar/labels/bracket-in-label-is-rejected
vectors.comment: A label containing a literal bracket could collide with Sec3.6.1's diagnostic-path convention, which appends [i] to a repeated label's second and later occurrences -- a repeatable field "a" and a separately-declared field literally named "a[1]" would both stringify to the path $.a[1] for genuinely different problems. Path is R (the label-itself-is-the-problem case), same convention as the empty-label vector.

vectors.name: osd-grammar/labels/closing-bracket-alone-in-label-is-rejected
vectors.comment: Either bracket character alone is enough to reject -- the rule is not specifically about a matched [i] pair, it's about the character vocabulary the diagnostic-path convention relies on being unambiguous.

vectors.name: osd-grammar/canonical-output/declaration-order-round-trips-exactly
vectors.comment: Sec3.3's canonical serialization order, principle 1: a read-side operation with nothing merged MUST preserve declaration order on write-back. Records are declared Z, A, R -- deliberately reverse-of-alphabetical -- specifically so this vector fails under an implementation that (wrongly) alphabetizes on write instead of preserving input order; a schema declared already-alphabetically would pass under either rule and prove nothing. Confirmed live against the Python reference before this vector was written: parse then immediate write reproduces Z, A, R exactly, not A, R, Z. This is a genuine new gap closed by this session's spec-correctness review, not carried-forward stale content -- Sec5.9's canonical-output claim existed long before any vector tested record order specifically.

vectors.name: osd-grammar/reserved-names/case-mismatched-name-is-not-reserved
vectors.comment: Sec3.3 S-3: the reserved-name check is exact and case-sensitive -- record String (capital S) does not collide with the string keyword. Characterization vector: all five ports already agreed on this behavior independently (verified 2026-09-13 by reading Python/TypeScript/Rust/Go/Java source, all plain case-sensitive equality, no case-folding anywhere) before S-3 stated it explicitly. Green-on-arrival everywhere, not a behavior change.

vectors.name: osd-grammar/strings/escaped-control-character-is-still-an-error
vectors.comment: Sec5.3.1's control-character ban applies to every raw byte in the string body, escape context included -- a control character immediately after a backslash is still a control character in the body. This was ambiguous until v0.15.0-beta: the prose said 'a literal control character', which invited the reading that only an unescaped one was forbidden, and grammars/osd.abnf's escape alternative was written as "\" %x00-10FFFF, which admitted the escaped form outright. So a parser generated from the grammar and one written from the prose disagreed on these exact bytes. Grammar and prose now agree and this vector pins it. The position was `1:1` until v0.19.0-beta, which is on line 1 (`record R {`) while the string is on line 2 and correct under no convention. Sec8.4's E-23 now states the convention the OML string-error vectors already followed: a string-body error reports the string's **opening quote**. Line 2 is four spaces then the quote, so the quote is at column 5 -- `2:5`. The reference reports a raw character offset (`18`) rather than a line:col here, which violates E-11; recorded as DIV-4.

vectors.name: osd-grammar/encoding/leading-bom-is-stripped
vectors.comment: D-15, the OSD half. A leading U+FEFF is consumed and contributes nothing to the Schema, exactly as on OML and the codecs; the result is identical to the same input without it, and grammars/osd.abnf admits BOM at offset zero and nowhere else. OSD was the third surface that rejected a BOM before D-15 -- measured against the reference, parse_schema raised SchemaError parse.unexpected-token -- alongside the JSON and TOML readers. Red against the reference by design, like its JSON and TOML counterparts.

vectors.name: osd-grammar/encoding/doubled-leading-bom-is-rejected
vectors.comment: D-21: D-15 consumes exactly one leading U+FEFF and stops. The text that remains is parsed by this surface's own grammar, which admits no U+FEFF as content at offset zero, so the second mark is a syntax error. The position is 1:1 because it is computed on the text remaining after the strip. The OSD half, companion to osd-grammar/encoding/leading-bom-is-stripped. Measured: the reference rejects it with the right code but reports the path as the raw offset `0` rather than a line:col, which E-11 forbids; recorded as DIV-4.
